o: Explain what UK copyright law protects.
Distinguish open-source and proprietary software licences.
Recommend a licence type using justified advantages and drawbacks.
c: The Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 protects many original works, including computer software. Copying or distributing protected software without appropriate permission or licence can infringe copyright.
A software licence sets out permissions and conditions for using, copying, modifying and distributing software. Owning or downloading a copy does not mean you can do anything with it.

Open-source licences allow people to inspect source code and usually to modify and redistribute it under specified licence conditions. Open source does not necessarily mean the software has no cost or conditions.

Proprietary software usually keeps the source code private and gives customers specified usage rights. It may offer vendor support, but users generally cannot modify or distribute the code without permission.

m.title: Select a suitable software licence
m.q: A club needs software it can adapt and inspect, but volunteers must follow licence rules. Explain why an open-source licence may suit it. [4 marks]
st: The club wants source-code access and customisation.
Open-source licensing provides access to source code [1] that can be inspected and modified [1].
This allows volunteers to adapt the software to their needs [1], provided they follow the terms of the chosen licence [1].
Avoid claiming all open-source software is free or that there are no conditions.

w: A museum wants to adapt the code of an exhibition app. Explain two benefits of open-source licensing. [4 marks]
Access to source code [1] lets developers inspect how the app works [1]. Permission to modify under the licence [1] allows it to be adapted for the museum's exhibits [1].
A company buys a proprietary graphics package with customer support. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of this choice. [4 marks]
Commercial/vendor support may be available [1], helping the company resolve issues [1]. Source code is usually unavailable [1], so the company cannot freely alter how the software works [1].
A pupil copies a paid game and shares it with a class without permission. Explain why this may breach copyright and the role of a licence. [4 marks]

The game is copyright-protected software [1]; copying/distributing it without permission may infringe the law [1]. The software licence specifies permitted use/distribution [1], and sharing outside those terms is not allowed [1].

k.q: Simulate a licence decision based on a permission flag; it does not enforce any actual licence.
k.code:
mayModify = 1
if mayModify == 1 then
    print("Changes permitted by licence")
else
    print("Check rights holder")
endif
p: Add print("Read the full licence") after the condition.
k.a:
Initially: Changes permitted by licence. When mayModify = 0: Check rights holder.

Extended OCR ERL:
mayModify = 0
if mayModify == 1 then
    print("Changes permitted by licence")
else
    print("Check rights holder")
endif
print("Read the full licence")

A flag is only a simulation; legal permissions depend on actual licence terms.

r: State one action prohibited by the Computer Misuse Act 1990. [1 mark]
State the overall purpose of the Data Protection Act 2018. [2 marks]
Regulates/protects the processing of personal data [1] and helps protect people's privacy/information rights [1].
What is meant by the colour depth of a bitmap image? [2 marks]
The number of bits used per pixel [1], determining how many possible colours each pixel can represent [1].
A school app requests pupils' names, emergency contacts and favourite music. Explain TWO data-protection responsibilities when collecting this information. [4 marks]
Identify and communicate a lawful, specific purpose [1], so people know why data is collected [1]. Minimise personal information collected [1], avoiding unnecessary items such as favourite music [1].
